props.title: Plague of the Zombies
props.initialSlug: Cornish village faces sinister voodoo zombie outbreak

sections.content: Plague of the Zombies (1966) stands as Hammer Horror's sole venture into zombie territory, predating Romero's Night of the Living Dead (1968) and offering a uniquely British take on the undead. Director John Gilling crafts a Victorian-era nightmare where aristocratic evil meets voodoo horror, creating a sharp commentary on class exploitation. The film's signature sequence - a nightmare featuring zombies rising from their graves in eerie green fog - influenced countless horror films that followed, including The Fog (1980) and The Serpent and the Rainbow (1988).

sections.content: The film's colonial undertones and class warfare themes emerge through its villain, Squire Hamilton, who uses voodoo to transform local villagers into undead mine workers. This exploitation narrative predates similar themes in Dawn of the Dead (1978) and provides a template for horror as social commentary. The film's Cornwall setting, with its foggy moors and ancient tin mines, creates a distinctly Gothic atmosphere that bridges classic Hammer horror with emerging zombie conventions.

Hammer's technical achievements shine throughout, particularly in the groundbreaking makeup effects by Roy Ashton. The zombies' blue-gray pallor and sunken eyes established a new visual standard for undead creatures, influencing everything from The Living Dead at Manchester Morgue (1974) to The Return of the Living Dead (1985). The film's voodoo elements connect it to earlier zombie works like I Walked with a Zombie (1943), while its themes of aristocratic evil align it with Hammer's broader Gothic catalog. sections.content: Unlike later zombie films focused on apocalyptic scenarios, Plague of the Zombies uses its undead as instruments of colonial power and class oppression. This approach influenced later British horror films like Blood on Satan's Claw (1971) and Witchfinder General (1968), which similarly examined power structures through horror. The film's focus on a rural community under siege from aristocratic evil became a template for folk horror, connecting it to films like The Wicker Man (1973).
